title: Jharkhand: Police fire tear gas at protesters seeking exam reforms
description: Police in India have fired tear gas shells on protesters demanding reforms to recruitment exams in the eastern state of Jharkhand.Thousands of student
body: Police in India have fired tear gas shells on protesters demanding reforms to recruitment exams in the eastern state of Jharkhand.Thousands of students, job seekers and volunteers have been trying to reach the state's assembly in the capital city of Ranchi to register their protest. The BBC has seen some people who have sustained injuries, though the official number of injured is unclear.The protesters have been demonstrating for over two weeks now, demanding an overhaul of Jharkhand's government exam system.On Monday, many attempted to breach police barricades, causing police to use water cannons, batons and tear gas to try and disperse crowds, officials say.Ranchi City Superintendent of Police Paras Rana told ANI news agency that most protesters had been peaceful, but accused a smaller group of breaking through barricades and throwing stones at officers. He said three policemen had been injured."About 90% of the students are peaceful, but there are some who are not listening even to their own representatives," he said.Rana said police had shown restraint and used "minimal force for a very short time" because the protesters were students. He appealed to them to remain peaceful, saying their demands were reaching the government.The protest comes weeks after thousands of young Indians attempted to march to the national parliament in Delhi, amid the massive "cockroach" protests over exam paper leaks.India's Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) - which is not a political party - called off its five-week-long protest on 25 July after education minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigned.The CJP had attracted support from students based in different states of the country.Meanwhile in Ranchi, visuals from the state capital show thousands of protesters, police as well as media personnel on the streets, amid tightened security arrangements.Despite police efforts to disperse them, large crowds remain at the site.Protesters in Jharkhand have been gathered at a stadium in Ranchi since 25 July - some have been sleeping in the open and several have gone on hunger strike.Even after multiple rounds of talks and the government accepting several demands, protesters say the agitation will continue until all their demands are met.The immediate cause of the anger is a preliminary civil service exam held by the Jharkhand Public Service Commission (JPSC) in April. After the results were announced in July, candidates alleged that leaked answer sheets shared on social media showed some successful applicants had answered far fewer questions than expected. This fuelled suspicions that the results had been manipulated. The state government has assured students that they will get justice. The allegations around the exam are being investigated by Jharkhand's Criminal Investigation Department (CID). More than a dozen people have been arrested.Investigators are also examining the role of a private company that conducted parts of the exam process after candidates raised questions about how it was selected.After talks with protesters on Sunday, the government agreed to cancel the exam in question, along with two others. Three JPSC members also reportedly resigned.This came after JPSC chairman L Khiangte stepped down on 22 July. He was questioned in the investigation and arrested on Monday.But protesters say several demands remain unmet, chief among them an investigation into the irregularities by the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI), India's premier federal investigative agency.

schema.headline: Jharkhand: Police fire tear gas at protesters seeking exam reforms

title: Drones spotted over German base days after Leipzig bomb incident
description: Two drones were spotted over a military base in western Germany just days after an explosive-laden device was found at Leipzig airport.Germany's armed
body: Two drones were spotted over a military base in western Germany just days after an explosive-laden device was found at Leipzig airport.Germany's armed forces (Bundeswehr) confirmed they were seen on Thursday evening at a base in Mechernich, near Bonn, reportedly housing components for US-made Patriot air-defence systems.A spokeswoman for the Bundeswehr Joint Force Command said military police were deployed to the site before the matter was handed over to local police.It is the latest instance of drones being spotted near military bases or airports in European nations supporting Ukraine in its war with Russia, on which suspicion has fallen. Moscow has consistently denied any involvement.German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt told newspaper Bild on Sunday that Germany had become a regular target of "destabilising" attacks."We're not at war, but we are the daily target of hybrid warfare," he said.Germany is currently investigating how a drone laden with explosives was able to reach a runway at Leipzig/Halle airport, which is used by Nato, the Germany military and serves as a base for Ukraine's Antonov Airlines.The Bundeswehr declined to comment on the ongoing investigation when asked by the BBC on Sunday about the suspected origins of the drones spotted above Mechernich.The local police force has been contacted for comment.German media reports that the base has a storage facility for equipment ​and spare parts used to maintain the Patriot missile batteries.The air-defence systems have become crucial to Ukraine's ability to intercept Russian ballistic missiles since Moscow's full-scale invasion began in 2022.However, President Volodymyr Zelensky this week pleaded to allies for further supplies, warning that Ukraine was running out of interceptor missiles.After initially offering Ukraine license to make Patriots in early July, US President Donald Trump last week denied any such agreement.A spate of drone sightings in European airspace last year left the continent on high alert, prompting the EU to discuss a continent-wide "drone wall" of air defences.Some European officials have blamed Russia for these drone sightings, claims Moscow has previously described as "absurd".

schema.headline: Drones spotted over German base days after Leipzig bomb incident

title: Ancient Roman shipwreck discovered off Sicily coast
description: Italian divers have discovered an ancient Roman shipwreck off the coast of Sicily, believed to be more than 2,000 years old.The vessel was found piled
body: Italian divers have discovered an ancient Roman shipwreck off the coast of Sicily, believed to be more than 2,000 years old.The vessel was found piled high with hundreds of well-preserved containers, which were used to transport goods such as wine and olive oil. Italy's Culture Minister Alessandro Giuli hailed the wreck as "one of the most important underwater archaeological discoveries of recent years".Specialist police divers found the ship around 46m (150ft) deep, after a tip-off from fishermen. The wreckage is 21m (69ft) long and 6m (20ft) wide, according to reports in local media.The culture ministry says it dates from the second or 1st Century BC. Fisherman and free-diver Giacomo De Mola described stumbling across the historic vessel while surveying the seabed near Mazara del Vallo.He wrote on social media that he had decided to dive and investigate after seeing something that appeared to be a large rock on his scanner. "I get closer. And my heart stops. It wasn't a rock," he said. Instead, he saw hundreds of amphorae - tall ceramic jars used to store goods in the ancient era, mostly wine, oil or grain."This is, without a doubt, the most incredible discovery of my life," he said. "It's hard to describe what it feels like to be among the first humans, in nearly 20 centuries, to see that place again."He posted a video of the wreck, showing eels, snappers and "countless marine life" living among the jars, noting: "The sea never ceases to amaze us. "This time we didn't just find a wreck, we found a piece of our history."

schema.headline: Ancient Roman shipwreck discovered off Sicily coast

title: The making of Auqib Nabi: Kashmir's hardships to India's Test cricket squad
description: How a schoolteacher's son became Kashmir's first India Test cricketerImage source, Abid BhatImage caption, Auqib replaced Jasprit Bumrah in the squad
body: How a schoolteacher's son became Kashmir's first India Test cricketerImage source, Abid BhatImage caption, Auqib replaced Jasprit Bumrah in the squad for the series against Sri Lanka beginning 15 AugustByMohsin KamalCricket writer"You play with so many cricket stars. Why don't you take selfies with them?"Bilal Ahmad Dar once asked his young cousin, Auqib Nabi.Auqib smiled and replied: "One day I will reach a place where they will want to take selfies with me."Years later, that prediction has come true.On Monday, the 29-year-old all-rounder became the first cricketer from Jammu and Kashmir to earn an India Test call-up after replacing Jasprit Bumrah in the squad for the two-match series against Sri Lanka, which starts on 15 August.For a region where conflict, harsh winters and limited infrastructure have long restricted sporting opportunities, Auqib's selection is being seen as a landmark moment.Raised in a small village in Baramulla district, Auqib grew up playing on local grounds with little infrastructure and few opportunities. His father, Ghulam Nabi Dar, a schoolteacher, initially wanted him to concentrate on academics and become a doctor.Image source, Abid BhatImage caption, Harsh winters and limited infrastructure have long restricted cricket in Kashmir"There was no scope in cricket. We used to think playing sport was a waste of time, so I insisted that Auqib focused on his studies," Ghulam says.But Auqib's persistence eventually changed his father's mind."After seeing his passion for cricket, I accepted it. I realised that, as a parent and a teacher, I shouldn't force him to do something he didn't want to do. I started supporting him."Auqib's childhood friend, Junaid Dar, remembers growing up in an environment where professional cricket barely seemed possible."Auqib was obsessed with cricket from childhood. I used to ask him, 'Why are you doing all this? There's no future in it.' We came from a place where there was no concept of playing sport professionally and hardly any infrastructure."To pursue his dream, Auqib regularly travelled around 70km (43 miles) to Srinagar to practise on proper cricket pitches. He did not even own a pair of spike shoes when he attended his first cricket trials.But his work ethic never changed, his cousin Bilal says."Auqib is very hardworking and consistent. He knows how to fight obstacles and make a way for himself."He would wake up early to go to the gym and then practise for the rest of the day. He did that almost every day for 10 years."Image source, NurPhoto via Getty Images)Image caption, A function to fete Auqib in Kashmir - he has become a local celebrityHis breakthrough came in 2020 when he made his Ranji Trophy (India's top domestic tournament) debut for Jammu and Kashmir, taking a five-wicket haul against Jharkhand.Former India all-rounder Parvez Rasool, Jammu and Kashmir's first international cricketer and Auqib's long-time captain, says one quality always stood out."I have followed Auqib's progress for a long time, and what stands out about him is his work ethic and discipline."Success, however, did not come overnight. Auqib claimed 44 wickets during the 2024-25 Ranji Trophy season, finishing as the competition's leading fast bowler, but remained largely outside the national conversation."When you do well but don't get recognition, it hurts," his father says."But we should never lose hope. Hope is what keeps the world intact. I always believed his time would come."It did.The following season, Auqib produced one of the finest bowling campaigns in recent Ranji Trophy history, taking 60 wickets in 10 matches to finish as the tournament's leading wicket-taker and help Jammu and Kashmir win their maiden Ranji Trophy title after a wait of 67 years.Image source, NurPhoto via Getty ImagesImage caption, Auqib produced one of the finest bowling campaigns in recent Ranji Trophy history, taking 60 wickets in 10 matchesThose performances earned him an 84m rupees (£730,000; $982,000) Indian Premier League (IPL) contract with Delhi Capitals. Although opportunities in the IPL were limited, his red-ball exploits had already caught the attention of India's selectors.For Rasool, Auqib's Test call-up carries significance far beyond one player."Playing Test cricket is the ultimate dream for any cricketer. It was my dream too. Seeing Auqib earn that call-up fills me with immense pride."In a way, it feels like a dream many of us in Jammu and Kashmir carried has finally been realised through him. It is a historic moment not just for Auqib and his family, but for cricket across the region."He believes Auqib's journey is remarkable not just because he reached the Indian team, but because of where he came from."Making it to the Indian team is incredibly difficult for any player, but the challenge is even greater when you come from Jammu and Kashmir. For years, we have had limited infrastructure, fewer opportunities and many obstacles that players from other parts of the country don't necessarily face."To reach this level, you need exceptional consistency, mental strength and the determination to keep believing in yourself. Auqib has shown all of those qualities, which is why this achievement is so special."Image source, Abid BhatImage caption, Auqib is also a useful lower-order batter Jammu and Kashmir became affiliated with the Board of Control for Cricket in India (BCCI) in 1957, yet the region still has only two major cricket stadiums, both with limited facilities. Long winters, heavy snowfall and decades of conflict have further slowed cricket's development."This is a landmark moment for cricket in Jammu and Kashmir," Rasool says."For a long time, people questioned whether someone from our region could make it to India's Test team. Auqib has answered that question. His selection shows players from Jammu and Kashmir can compete with the best if they are given the opportunity."He believes Auqib's journey will inspire a new generation."When I started playing, there weren't many role models from Jammu and Kashmir. Today, things are changing."Auqib becoming the first player from the region to earn an India Test call-up will give countless youngsters the belief that they can dream big too. His journey proves that no matter where you come from or what challenges you face, hard work and perseverance can take you to the highest level."Back in Baramulla, Ghulam Nabi now finds himself recognised everywhere he goes."People come up to me, hug me and say, 'This is Auqib's father.'"It makes me immensely proud."

schema.headline: The making of Auqib Nabi: Kashmir's hardships to India's Test cricket squad

title: Israel rejects Trump's 15-point plan for Gaza, Netanyahu says
description: Image source, Getty ImagesIsraeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has rejected US President Donald Trump's 15-point plan for Gaza, stating that no m
body: Image source, Getty ImagesIsraeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has rejected US President Donald Trump's 15-point plan for Gaza, stating that no military pull-out will happen until Hamas is "genuinely" disarmed.Trump's Board of Peace said last month it had reached an agreement for the "complete disarmament" of Hamas and other armed groups in Gaza.But Hamas said handing over its heavy weapons was contingent on Israel ending "all forms of aggression" and withdrawing its forces from Gaza.On Sunday, a senior Board of Peace official insisted the US-backed peace plan for the territory remained the only way forward.Israel has continued to carry out strikes on Gaza since agreeing to an initial ceasefire in the territory last October."Israel rejects the 15-point document," Netanyahu said at a cabinet meeting on Sunday.The Israeli military "will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is genuinely disarmed and will continue to thwart threats against our forces and our citizens", he added. A Hamas official told the BBC on Sunday the group "reaffirms it commitment" to the agreement and it was ready "to engage seriously and responsibly in implementing" the 15-point plan.They called on mediators to ensure "that all parties comply with what has been agreed".Israel's rejection signals another blow for Trump's Gaza peace plan which was announced in September last year.The plan included the creation of the Board of Peace to oversee the agreement's implementation, as well as the disarmament of Hamas, withdrawal of Israeli troops and reconstruction of Gaza.Netanyahu's statement does not come as a surprise. But he has taken some time to make it, perhaps reflecting the difficult position the Israeli leader is in.He clearly is unhappy with Trump's plan but at the same time he will not want to upset his closest ally.It's just over a week since Trump announced what he called a "monumental step toward lasting peace and security" - that Hamas for the first time had agreed to disarm, on condition that Israel withdraws its forces from Gaza.On Sunday, Netanyahu was clear that was not going to happen under his watch. He said Hamas had to disarm first, adding that it couldn't be some "fictitious disarmament" - it had to be real.The reality is any disarmament and withdrawal of Israeli forces would likely need to be phased.Netanyahu said he was now in discussion with US officials about how to go forward. "They have ideas; some of them are acceptable to us and some are not, and we know how to stand our ground on these matters," he said.But just months before Israeli elections and under pressure from members of his right-wing coalition to take a tough stance on Gaza, he is unlikely to want to make concessions.He has faced calls from far-right parts of the coalition to hold a new cabinet vote and end the Gaza plan, including National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir who dismissed the draft as "not acceptable".Figure caption, Large crowds turned out in Gaza City on Tuesday for a mass funeral for 112 people, mostly women and children, who were killed in an Israeli strike on a residential block in late 2023Nickolay Mladenov - a senior diplomat tasked with implementing Donald Trump's peace plan - defended the plan on Sunday and said discussions were ongoing in the hope of a "positive outcome".The board's high representative for Gaza told Israel's Channel 12 that Israel had been asked "to give the process a chance" and said the plan was "the only way forward" to ensure there was no repeat of the 7 October 2023 attack by Hamas.Mladenov said the plan was built on a process that was "verifiable, that is reversible, that at each stage can be stopped, and that we have built up with a very clear-eyed understanding of what are the challenges ahead".He also said that Israel would not be required to withdraw until it could be verified that Hamas was taking steps to disarm.According to the United Nations, about 1.9 million people - 90% of Gaza's population - have been displaced in the territory since the war in Gaza started. The war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, in which about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.Israel responded to the attack by launching a military campaign in Gaza, during which more than 73,000 people have been killed, according to the territory's health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations.Additional reporting by Jack Burgess

schema.headline: Israel rejects Trump's 15-point plan for Gaza, Netanyahu says

title: Nigeria's mass wedding - and how to tell lovers from fraudsters in Kano
description: Celebrations have turned the northern Nigerian city of Kano into a riot of colour and excitement over the last week as 1,500 couples married at a mass
body: Celebrations have turned the northern Nigerian city of Kano into a riot of colour and excitement over the last week as 1,500 couples married at a mass wedding.For days the city's streets have been buzzing with bridal parties and their families preparing outfits and attending other organised events.On Friday, brides in red hijabs with grooms in matching red hats and white robes went to the palace of the Emir, the city's traditional Muslim leader, for the main ceremony where they officially became husband and wife.The nuptials culminated on Saturday with a wedding breakfast hosted by Governor Abba Kabir Yusuf, who offered his blessing to the newlyweds.The Kano state government sponsored this initiative, spending 1.5bn naira ($1m; £815,000) to support those tying the knot - providing the bride's dowry and furniture for the couple's first home.The scheme targets low-income individuals who cannot afford the significant financial costs associated with marriage.The annual event was initiated in 2012 by the then-governor when 100 couples - primarily widows and divorcees - wed at the palace.The mass weddings have continued under subsequent governors, with numbers expanding each year as demand has grown and included those in polygamous Muslim marriages.Such is the popularity of the scheme that 5,000 couples applied this year.The event is always overseen by the Hisbah - the city's Islamic police force - and one of their main tasks is to vet the couples wanting to wed.Kano has a majority Muslim population and Sharia operates in the state alongside the secular legal system.Mujahid Aminudeen, deputy commander-general of the Hisbah, admits it is not an easy task."Whenever we find out that there's something dubious or fishy about a couple, we disqualify them," he tells the BBC.He says some couples will go to great lengths to convince the authorities that they are a genuine love match when their eye is more on the benefits on offer.The state government has spent approximately 1m naira ($735; £544) on each participating couple.According to the Hisbah, the support package a couple receives includes essential household items needed to establish a new home: beds, mattresses, bedsheets, pillows, furniture and food supplies.Each bride receives a dowry of 100,000 naira, while a further 100,000 naira is provided as start-up capital to encourage small-scale entrepreneurship and help the couple achieve financial self-reliance after marriage.All intending couples must undergo comprehensive medical examinations - including tests for HIV, hepatitis, pregnancy and genotype compatibility - before being cleared for the programme.Aminudeen revealed that some couples had been disqualified after being discovered to have altered their medical test results.In one case, an intending bride was found to have presented her brother as the groom in an attempt to benefit from the scheme.Local journalist Yusuf Ali Abdallah, who has covered the mass weddings for years, said Nigeria's struggling economy had been fuelling desperation among the applicants this year."As we all know, marriage involves spending money and the country's economy is not bright at the moment," he told the BBC."This makes some people desperate to get on this list."One couple who were already married had even attempted to present themselves as an intending pair before being detected and removed from the programme, he said.Other charlatans have tried to take advantage of those desperate to get on the sponsored list, which was made public two weeks ago.One Kano resident, who asked to be anonymous, said he had been asked to pay a bribe to get on the list."But to be fair to the organisers, I later found out those who asked me for money were not Hisbah staff," he said.He and his fiancée failed to be chosen for this August's wedding but he said he would try again next year.Aminudeen admitted that the Islamic police were aware of such allegations: "We have found that there are some people asking others to pay certain money so they can make the list."But the Hisbah officer wanted to assure all those wishing to wed in future that the entire process should not cost them a single naira."We want to announce to the people of Kano that the whole process is free: from the selection to the medicals and the goods set aside for couples - all are covered by the government."One of successful grooms, 43-year-old clothes trader Rabiu Yusuf, agreed the process of applying to be married had gone smoothly for him."Personally, no-one asked me for anything. I was told the government would sponsor it all," he told the BBC.His new wife is Aisha Auwal - the couple met as she regularly visited his shop to buy clothes.Yusuf, who already has five children with his first wife, said he was "very happy and can't wait to start a new life" with his customer-turned-bride.24 year-old Amina Alhassan echoed his sentiments, adding that she had not encountered any problems when applying to marry 40-year-old Nura Abdullahi.Their union was first arranged by their families in Dambatta village before they presented themselves to the Hisbah."Everything has been free and I want to commend the Kano government for this scheme because without it, many couldn't have afforded to marry due to the high cost of living."After Saturday's wedding feast, the presentation of the household goods began.But it will take several more days for the excitement to die down in Kano and as the newlyweds busy themselves with setting up home together.

schema.headline: Nigeria's mass wedding - and how to tell lovers from fraudsters in Kano

title: Daniel Kinahan: Suspected crime boss Kinahan spends first night in custody in Ireland
description: Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Daniel Kinahan (far right) was escorted to and from the court under heavy police guardByGabija GataveckaiteReport
body: Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Daniel Kinahan (far right) was escorted to and from the court under heavy police guardByGabija GataveckaiteReporting fromreporting from Dublin's Special Criminal CourtEimear Flanagan and Barry O'ConnorBBC News NIUpdated 3 hours agoSuspected crime boss Daniel Kinahan, one of the world's most wanted men, has spent his first night in custody in Ireland after being extradited from Dubai.The 49-year-old appeared before Dublin's Special Criminal Court court on Sunday for a 13-minute non-jury hearing, where he was remanded in custody until 5 October.He has been charged with directing the activities of a criminal organisation between 18 October 2015 and 6 April 2017.When it was explained to Kinahan that he could file an application for bail through the High Court, he replied: "I think we all know I won't be getting bail, but thank you for your time."An Irish government jet carrying Kinahan landed in Dublin after 18:00 local time. He was arrested and charged upon his arrival.Heavy police operationAfter his arrival and arrest at Baldonnell Casement Aerodrome on Sunday evening, he was directly transported under heavy police guard to the Criminal Courts of Justice in Dublin.All the benches were full in a packed courtroom of journalists, a number of solicitors from the Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP), some members of the public and court clerks.In court, Kinahan was sitting on a wooden bench and wearing a black hooded top.He appeared before judges Patrick McGrath, Sarah Berkeley and Fiona Lydon, and rose to his feet when the three judges took their places.Image source, PA MediaImage caption, A police convoy escorted Kinahan at speed to the courtKinahan did not have legal representation, and told the court that he did not have time to arrange this.When Judge McGrath suggested that he should be charged today and legal representation arranged later on, Kinahan replied: "If I have time, yes."Det Sgt Colm Davison told the court he arrested Kinahan earlier that evening.Judge McGrath asked Kinahan if he would like to appear at the next court sitting in person or via videolink.Kinahan asked if he had to "decide now" and it was explained to him he could make a decision later and notify the governor in the prison.Image source, Mike O'DonnellImage caption, An artist's impression of Kinahan during his hearing on SundayA large-scale security operation was in place ahead of Sunday's hearing.Ahead of the extradition, the Irish Prison Service bought a bulletproof and bombproof van which can be used to escort prisoners who are considered high-risk.Garda Commissioner Justin Kelly said the arrest shows the force's determination to "target transnational organised crime groups" alongside international policing partners such as Dubai police.He added it shows the value of the force's relationship with the authorities in the UAE, the Irish ministry of justice at judicial level, and "on a police-to-police basis".Who is Daniel Kinahan?Kinahan was arrested in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) in April. He appealed the extradition order over the past few months but his attempts were unsuccessful.The National Crime Agency (NCA) has previously said that the Kinahan cartel has been responsible for importing tonnes of drugs and firearms around the world and has also been linked to more than a dozen gangland murders.Kinahan was not only wanted by the authorities in Ireland - the US Treasury Department once described the Kinahan cartel as one of the most dangerous in the world.Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Daniel Kinahan arrived into Casement Aerodrome in Baldonnel, Dublin on the government jet on Sunday eveningThe US government imposed sanctions on Kinahan in April 2022 after identifying him and other members of his family as leaders of the Kinahan organised crime cartel.He fought attempts to extradite him back to his native country, where the Kinahan cartel was involved in a long-running gangland feud that claimed 18 lives.On 5 February 2016, an attempt was made on Kinahan's life in what became known as the Regency Hotel shooting.One of his associates, David Byrne, was shot dead, while two others were shot and injured.This incident was part of what became known as the Hutch-Kinahan feud.Kinahan also had ties to the world of sport via his now defunct boxing management company MTK Global, which represented more than 100 boxers including Tyson Fury and Carl Frampton.'Landmark of judicial cooperation'The UAE and Ireland have an extradition treaty and on Sunday justice ministers from both jurisdictions issued a joint statement welcoming Kinahan's extradition."The Irish national is regarded as one of the most high-profile individuals sought for prosecution in connection with transnational organised crime and is accused of directing an organised crime organisation," it stated.Irish Justice Minister Jim O'Callaghan described the extradition as a "landmark of judicial cooperation between the two countries".He also commended "the professionalism, efficiency, and diligence demonstrated by the UAE judicial authorities throughout the extradition proceedings".His UAE counterpart, Abdullah bin Sultan bin Awad Al Nuaimi, said it underscored "the steadfast commitment we have to supporting global efforts to combat transnational organised crime". The extradition agreement was previously used to extradite Sean McGovern, a "senior lieutenant" in the Kinahan organised crime group.He was sentenced to 24 years in prison in June for directing the activities of a criminal organisation.What is the Kinahan cartel?According to former Garda Commissioner Drew Harris, the gang is estimated to have made more than €1bn (£857,870,000) globally from its activities.The US Treasury Department has in the past compared the gang to crime organisations such as Italy's Camorra, Mexico's Los Zetas and Japan's Yakuza.A reward of up to $5m (£3.7m) has also been offered by the US for information on Daniel, his father Christopher Snr and brother Christopher Jnr.Image source, CAROLINE QUINN/GETTY IMAGESImage caption, Gangland rivals tried to shoot Daniel Kinahan during a boxing weigh-in event in Dublin's Regency Hotel 10 years agoIn 2022, Thomas Kavanagh, who the NCA said ran the group's criminal operations in the UK, was jailed for 21 years alongside Gary Vickery and Daniel Canning, who were sentenced to 20 years and 19 and a half years respectively.The NCA said evidence showed they were responsible for cocaine imports estimated to be up to £23.4m, and cannabis imports worth about £6.4m.Kinahan himself became a target for murder and escaped an attempt on his life during a fatal shooting at a Dublin hotel in 2016.He left Ireland and spent time living in Spain and more recently in Dubai, where a warrant for his arrest was issued by the Irish courts in April. Daniel Kinahan's lawyer previously told BBC Panorama that he has no criminal record or convictions and allegations about him being a crime boss are false and have no evidential basis.

schema.headline: Daniel Kinahan: Suspected crime boss Kinahan spends first night in custody in Ireland

title: Evidence that South African special forces murdered top detective shared with BBC
description: Senior police detective Frans Mathipa had been fighting for four months to gain access to a crucial piece of information in the case he was working on
body: Senior police detective Frans Mathipa had been fighting for four months to gain access to a crucial piece of information in the case he was working on. Finally, he was told, it was going to come his way.But he feared his pursuit of it could cost him his life.Two days later, his car was found overturned - he had been shot dead while driving.Now seven members of South Africa's special forces, and one military police officer, have been charged with murdering Lt Col Mathipa, a highly respected officer, in August 2023. They deny the charges.There has been no date scheduled for their trial, and there are concerns it will never go ahead, because three of the men charged with his murder have refused to comply with a court order revoking their bail. They are still working for the army's special forces, and one of them has been promoted.The BBC World Service has been given exclusive access to the prosecution case against all the men.The case has caused consternation in one of Africa's most robust democracies, with fears the country's military is significantly overreaching its mandate.We asked the South African army whether it was responsible for Mathipa's killing. It did not respond.Several hundred pages of secret police and court documents, shared with the BBC, set out the evidence suggesting special forces killed Mathipa - who worked for an elite police unit known as "The Hawks".We have also interviewed key sources in the police investigation - South Africa's former head of counter-terrorism in The Hawks; Mathipa's commanding officer; and Mathipa's family - to build the most comprehensive public account of the events leading up to the detective's death.It presents a compelling case that South Africa's special forces are responsible for his murder.In particular, police documents show that the vehicle that trailed Mathipa just before he was shot was registered to a front company for the special forces. And that tracking data found in that vehicle puts it at the scene of the shooting.One of the men in the car, Maj Sunnybooi Wambi, the documents show, was also spotted at the scene of an alleged abduction carried out by special forces soldiers -  the case that Mathipa had been investigating.After Mathipa's death, special forces issued a chilling warning to The Hawks, the police documents say. "You can appoint 10 investigating officers; we will kill all of them," said the warning, according to police.Outside the UK watch on YouTube, externalThe case Mathipa had been investigating was sensitive.It centred on an Ethiopian man called Abdella Abadigga, an alleged so-called Islamic State [IS] militant. He had been granted temporary asylum in South Africa in 2008, but was arrested abroad in 2017.Abadigga had then been smuggled back into the country, by the South African military and Department of Home Affairs, to be used as an intelligence asset - but had "gone rogue", according to Col Tollie Vreugdenburg, former head of counter-terrorism in The Hawks. Abadigga had gone on to extort Johannesburg's Ethiopian neighbourhood, sources in the community told us. This money was used to fund IS, says the US government.We asked the South African army if it had facilitated Abadigga's return to South Africa. And we asked the Department of Home Affairs if it had lied about a planned deportation of him to Ethiopia, and had instead smuggled him back into South Africa on an expired passport and refugee permit. They did not respond.Specifically, Mathipa was investigating the allegation that special forces had then gone on to abduct and kill Abadigga in December 2022 - who the United States, earlier that year, had put under sanctions, designating him an IS recruiter and fundraiser, as well as a trusted supporter of Bilal al-Sudani, a top IS figure in Somalia.Court documents show that after Abadigga's abduction, his phone connected to a mast near a military base. Police sources say it was used to call a number in Somalia.The Pentagon did not respond to the BBC's question on whether Abadigga's phone helped locate al-Sudani, who was killed by US special forces in Somalia in January 2023, only a few weeks after Abadigga's alleged abduction.We also asked South Africa's President Cyril Ramaphosa whether Abadigga had been kidnapped at the behest of the US. He declined to comment.When Mathipa was assigned the case, four months before his own death, he already knew special forces were implicated, but he was trying to secure more evidence.He was building on information already gathered by Abadigga's brother, Ameen - who had opened a missing person's case soon after the disappearance, and had been assigned an investigating officer (IO) from local police.He and the IO had obtained CCTV footage showing the last known movements of Abadigga and his bodyguard Kadir Abotese at the Mall of Africa, a shopping centre on the outskirts of Johannesburg.The footage, clips of which the BBC has seen, shows a man in a blue top following Abadigga and his bodyguard as they leave the food court to head back to the car park, and paying for parking three seconds after Abadigga and Abotese do.The mall CCTV footage contains another vital clue. The licence plates of the suspected kidnappers' vehicles are clearly visible.The vehicles were all registered to a company called Peters Communications Trust (PCT), a front company for South African special forces - Ameen and the IO were to discover.At the time of Abadigga's disappearance, PCT's directors included Maj Gen Herbert Mashego, the then commanding officer of 5 Special Forces Regiment.Police documents say a meeting was arranged between the IO and high ranks of the military, including Brig Gen Yalo, the then head of special forces, at which the IO was instructed to tell Ameen there was no link between PCT and the military.So, with the investigation seemingly at a standstill, Abadigga's brother took his case to the Johannesburg High Court.Responding to Ameen's legal action, special forces denied all knowledge of Abadigga or his whereabouts. They did, however, admit their soldiers had been at the Mall of Africa on the date in question, but said they had been there for a training exercise.They named the man seen wearing blue on CCTV as Maj Sunnybooi Wambi, and said he had been the exercise commander. They also admitted all the suspect vehicles seen at the mall belonged to them.Domestic operations by South Africa's military need to be authorised by both the government and the presidency.We asked South African former Defence Minister Thandi Modise, and President Ramaphosa, if they had authorised a training exercise in the Mall of Africa - Modise did not respond and Ramaphosa declined to comment.When Mathipa was assigned to the case a month later, he issued a subpoena to special forces to force them to hand over full details of this alleged training exercise and all the personnel involved.When access to these documents was finally promised, three months later, Mathipa had a premonition that he would be murdered - according to Brig Paulina Sekgobela, his commanding officer."When [Mathipa] left my office he said: 'Brigadier, you know, these people - they are going to kill me. I'm going to die'," she told the BBC.On the day Mathipa was killed, he was phoned by a man calling himself Tebogo, who claimed he had information on the case for the detective - according to Mathipa's daughter Basetsana, who was home with him at the time.Mathipa and Tebogo arranged to meet at a petrol station in Pretoria.When Tebogo failed to show, Mathipa drove away again, along the highway.He was killed while driving, by rounds fired from high-velocity weapons which special forces would have had access to, according to South African police.And footage from motorway toll gantries, police say, shows one of the occupants of the black BMW, which tailed Mathipa moments before his murder, was Maj Sunnybooi Wambi.This car, like the three vehicles connected with Abadigga's disappearance at the mall, was registered to PCT, they add.New detectives were assigned to the case after Mathipa's death, triggering a chilling message from special forces, that made its way to the police's Criminal Intelligence division.Police say it warned that, however many investigating officers were assigned to the case, "we will kill all of them".Twelve members of the South African military have been arrested in total, including Lt Col Sunnybooi Wambi, and the current head of South Africa's special forces, Brig Gen Solomon Lechoenyo - both promoted to these positions since police first started investigating their roles in the case.The 12 have been variously charged with the abduction and murder of Abadigga and Abotese, the murder of Mathipa, fraud, and obstruction.All deny all charges and they were initially released on bail. But six of them later had their bail revoked, and were ordered to turn themselves in to custody.Three of the six, including Wambi, have been charged with both Mathipa's murder, and Abotese's abduction and murder.

schema.headline: Evidence that South African special forces murdered top detective shared with BBC

title: Alleged rebel leader killed in Colombia as president targets armed groups
description: Military intelligence officers said that Forero led a group known as Frente 28, which is one of the many dissident factions to have sprung forth from
body: Military intelligence officers said that Forero led a group known as Frente 28, which is one of the many dissident factions to have sprung forth from the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (Farc).The Farc, Colombia's largest left-wing rebel group, signed a peace deal with the  government in 2016 but some of its members did not agree to the terms of the deal and refused to lay down their arms.These dissidents groups, which are now mainly involved in cocaine trafficking and illegal mining, are among the main driving forces behind the resurgence in violence in the country.  De la Espriella said he would take a radically different approach to defeating criminal groups in the country than his predecessor in office, Gustavo Petro. Petro, the first left-wing politician to be elected president of Colombia, advocated what he called a "total peace" strategy, which prioritised negotiation over confrontation. His attempts to negotiate with a number of armed groups, however, failed as members of the illegal organisations repeatedly broke ceasefires and walked away from the talks. De la Espriella's combative approach has been met with defiance by dissident rebel groups. On Saturday, just a day after the was sworn into office, two explosive devices went off.In Cauca province, a car bomb exploded at a tollbooth, injuring two security guards, and in Cesar province, a police officer was killed by explosives dropped from a drone. In a video uploaded to social media, de la Espriella praised the military for killing Forero, who was also known as "El ruso" (The Russian), and whom he described as an explosives expert.He added that three more alleged members of the dissident group had been killed in the military operation in a rural area in Meta province. The president also said that soldiers had killed two alleged members of another criminal group, the Gulf Clan, in a separate offensive in Antioquia province. De la Espriella has the backing of US President Donald Trump, who endorsed his candidacy.On Friday, the US state department said it planned to provide $1bn (£740m) in security assistance to de la Espriella's government.It also welcomed Colombia into the US-led group dubbed "Shield of the Americas" - an alliance of Western Hemisphere countries which have pledged to co-operate in their fight against drug trafficking gangs and transnational crime.

schema.headline: Alleged rebel leader killed in Colombia as president targets armed groups

title: Chalong Riewrang: Former Thai MP allegedly kills official and confesses on YouTube
description: A former Thai MP allegedly shot dead a local official in the southern province of Nonthaburi, then dialled into a YouTube livestream to inform the hos
body: A former Thai MP allegedly shot dead a local official in the southern province of Nonthaburi, then dialled into a YouTube livestream to inform the host - a political pundit - of what he had done.Former Nonthaburi MP Chalong Reawraeng told the shocked host, Anchalee Paireerak, that he had shot Thongchai Yenprasert, a former police official, outside Thongchai's office.Thongchai, who was hit in the neck, died in hospital. His driver was shot in the arm and hand.Chalong was arrested but then allowed to hold a press conference at a police station where he attempted to explain what had happened while smoking a cigarette. He told the reporters there that Thongchai was "angry" at him, but did not explain why. He also said he did not intend to shoot Thongchai, whom he described as a "good friend".Chalong said he told Thongchai that he wanted to talk to him. According to local media reports, the two were involved in a personal dispute."He [Thongchai] then pushed me, saying 'I don't want to talk, I don't want to talk.'"Chalong said he then followed Thongchai towards his car."When I pulled the gun out, I didn't intend to shoot him. But then [Thongchai's driver] pulled his gun out and pointed it at me, so I fired."Thongchai, a retired police colonel, was president of the Nonthaburi Provincial Administrative Organisation or PAO, a local government body.Earlier, Chalong had called political commentator Anchalee Paireerak, who was livestreaming on YouTube at the time, to confess to the incident.Anchalee was filmed picking up a call midway through her programme. "I'll call you back... Oh, something big [happened]? Go ahead, what's that?" she said.Viewers could not hear what the caller said next, but Anchalee was seen reacting in shock."Did he die? Did he die? You shot him in the head? You need to wait there for the cops," she said on the video, which was seen by the BBC. "Don't go anywhere."Monday's shooting came three days after a 14-year-old boy shot dead eight people at his home and school, then killed himself, in Thailand's worst mass shooting since 2022. The two attacks are not related.The latest shooting will further spur debate about gun control in Thailand, which has the highest rate of gun ownership in South East Asia by a wide margin.After Friday's school shooting, Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul ordered tougher enforcement of gun laws and said police would set up checkpoints as part of a crackdown.Other measures would include tightening controls on the possession, carrying and use of firearms.

schema.headline: Chalong Riewrang: Former Thai MP allegedly kills official and confesses on YouTube

title: Hundreds arrested over French wildfires, but who is to blame?
description: After wildfires caused more damage in France this year than at any time since World War Two, many are left asking a single question: why?A major drive
body: After wildfires caused more damage in France this year than at any time since World War Two, many are left asking a single question: why?A major driver is that climate is changing as a result of the well-documented way humanity is burning fossil fuels. Temperatures are only rising.But with records showing that nine out of 10 French wildfires are started by humans, the government in Paris is trying to attribute blame - although it is itself accused of being underprepared for the infernos that have now scorched more than 300,000 acres this summer.The interior ministry has announced 420 arrests of people alleged to have either started the fires deliberately or by accident. Among them are 166 minors.In one case, a 23-year-old man has been accused of deliberately starting 10 fires in the space of five days in the south-eastern Var area last month. He faces 15 years in prison and a €150,000 (£128,000) fine, if convicted.Many others have been tried and immediately sentenced, such as a man who received a three-year jail sentence for starting three recent fires in the Raon-L'Étape forest in the Vosges region. "Only a few square metres of vegetation went up in smoke," noted L'Est Républicain, the newspaper that reported the story.Other prosecutions have been perceived as heavy-handed and unjust. A homeless man and someone with severe autism have reportedly been handed jail terms for throwing cigarette butts."I was amazed at the number of arrests, it feels excessive," admits Muriel Gestas, a lawyer who has represented several people accused of arson, including two firefighters. She doubts many will lead to a conviction.The newspaper Le Monde is also unconvinced. It questions to what extent police have examined these cases, given the short time frame.The authorities' silence on the details - the specific charges, notably whether they involve intent and how the numbers compare with past seasons - rules out any meaningful comparison with previous years, it argues.But Bordeaux prosecutor Renaud Gaudeul told Le Monde that a tough approach was justified by current circumstances. "The conditions for a charge of endangering lives are met for those who throw a cigarette butt or light a barbecue in wooded areas. It only takes a tiny spark for it to start," the newspaper quoted him as saying. Working out how a fire started is, unsurprisingly, not easy."In periods of drought such as this one, all you need is a simple lighter," explains Eric Dufayet, an officer who investigates fires.Once a fire is out, Eric's first task is to map its outline along the edge of the burnt vegetation, then trace it back to its point of origin. If the wind has been steady, that outline often forms a "V" shape. From there, his team works backwards along the path the flames took."If someone deliberately starts a fire, they may not have used only one device," he says. It improves the chances of a DNA or fingerprint sample being found.Experts believe arson accounts for only a small fraction of fires. Most are believed to be accidental, with sparks potentially coming from construction work, faulty electrical equipment, cigarette butts and barbecues."With cigarettes, it's called the '30' rule," says Eric Dufayet. To start a fire, he explains, there must be "a temperature of at least 30C (86F), a maximum of 30% humidity, wind of less than 30km/h (19mph), and at least 30% of the cigarette unburnt."In the current drought, he says it is even easier. If those conditions are met, a fire can easily spread, and fast.According to Michel Lejoyeux, a professor of psychiatry and addictive behaviour at Paris 7 University, people who start fires fall into three categories: those who are careless, those who benefit - with an insurance payout, for example - and pyromaniacs."The pyromaniac doesn't get money, has no spirit of revenge, has no utility of the fire, but he likes the fire," he says.However, pyromania is a rare psychiatric disorder that Lejoyeux says is very difficult to diagnose, and accounts for few arson convictions.Lawyer Muriel Gestas, who has handled several such cases, says some firefighters alleged to have started fires may have wanted to be seen as saviours. For others - notably volunteers earning tax-free overtime - the motive may be financial.Amid concerns over how officials are pursuing suspects, broader worries about wildfires are far from abating. Forecasts suggest France's next heatwave is only days away.President Emmanuel Macron says criticism should not be the priority right now. "We will have to replant and rebuild a different kind of forest because we must adapt to the structural conditions of climate change," he said this week."The time for reviewing lessons learned will come," he insisted. "In the meantime, the country must remain united."Even so, the damage these fires have inflicted on the environment, hundreds of homes, tourism, local businesses and air quality has left the French public with a lot of questions.

schema.headline: Hundreds arrested over French wildfires, but who is to blame?

title: Battle for Mali base has killed dozens of militants, army says
description: The authorities in Mali say their soldiers killed dozens of militant Islamists as they repelled an attack on a military base on Sunday.Jama'at Nusrat
body: The authorities in Mali say their soldiers killed dozens of militant Islamists as they repelled an attack on a military base on Sunday.Jama'at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM), a jihadist group affiliated to al-Qaeda, said it was behind the assault where its fighters took control of the base in the town of San.The army, which also suffered casualties, disputed it had ceded control - but said its soldiers had to "retreat temporarily".It comes as Mali's security situation appears to be deteriorating, more than a decade after a jihadist insurgency began taking root in the north of the country."The enemy was eliminated and the attack was successfully repelled. Around 40 terrorists were eliminated," Lt Col El Oumrani, the commander of the 23rd regiment in the San garrison, said in a video.He urged residents to remain vigilant, insisting that his soldiers had "not gone anywhere" and the base remained under army control."The camp of the 23rd is not empty, it is under the custody of the army."The attack started at around 05:00 local time (GMT) on Sunday and lasted for about two hours, according to witnesses quoted by the French broadcaster RFI.The attackers came on motorcycles and on foot, some disguised in army uniforms to infiltrate the base, RFI reported the witnesses as saying.One said the militants entered the camp and held it "for a long time before leaving"."I noticed that the fighting took place between 200 and 300 metres from the camp. Several terrorists were killed by soldiers, but others fled; some even hid in houses and others went into the forest," the witness said.At least 10 soldiers were killed in the fighting and the assailants briefly took over the camp, the AFP news agency quoted security and local sources.The army told national broadcaster ORTM that the militants used drones, heavy machine guns and armoured vehicles to breach the site's perimeter.Since 2012, Mali has been plagued by insurgencies and large parts of the north and east of the country remain outside government control.April saw nationwide, co-ordinated attacks by an alliance of jihadists and separatist rebels in the north - the Azawad Liberation Front - seeking to overthrow the military regime of Gen Assimi Goïta, who seized power in a coup in 2020.During the attacks, Defence Minister Sadio Camara was killed in an apparent suicide truck bombing on his residence near the capital, Bamako.JNIM has diversified its operations and begun targeting not only northern Mali but also central and southern Mali, showing an ability to penetrate deeper into the territory despite numerous military operations.In the wake of the coup, which was in part carried out over the failure to ease the security situation, Mali rejected French military help and instead turned to Russia.Additional reporting by BBC Monitoring

schema.headline: Battle for Mali base has killed dozens of militants, army says

title: Typhoon Dolphin: China evacuates more than 1 million people as massive storm arrives
description: Chinese authorities have evacuated more than a million people from their homes in eastern China including the financial capital Shanghai, as Typhoon D
body: Chinese authorities have evacuated more than a million people from their homes in eastern China including the financial capital Shanghai, as Typhoon Dolphin made landfall.The typhoon brought heavy rain and halted transportation across the region. Nearly 1,000 flights were cancelled in Shanghai alone on Monday.While authorities have downgraded Dolphin to a tropical storm, they continue to warn of torrential rains, severe flooding and the risk of landslides through to Wednesday as the storm moves north.Chinese authorities had earlier issued their highest-level red alert for Dolphin, which is the strongest storm to hit China this year.It packed maximum wind speeds of 150km/h (94mph) when it first slammed into Yuhuan in the Zhejiang province at 17:30 (09:30 GMT) on Sunday before making a second landfall in the city of Wenzhou about an hour later, meteorological authorities said.Heavy rain was forecast on Monday for the provinces of Shandong, Henan, Hubei, Anhui, Jiangsu, Zhejiang and the city of Shanghai.Governments have urged people to avoid outdoor activities, while several top tourist attractions remain closed, including parts of Disneyland and Legoland, and several viewing platforms along the Bund in Shanghai.Footage on state media show ground-floor businesses flooded in the former French Concession in Shanghai, an area popular with tourists, and people wading through ankle-deep waters.Several state media outlets have reported that a nine-year-old boy from Wenling, Zhejiang is missing after being swept into the sea. Chinese officials have not reported any casualties.Parts of Zhejiang could receive 250mm to 500mm of rain over the next few days, forecasters say.Authorities in Hangzhou, Zhejiang's capital city, have waived parking fees in all public spaces for drivers seeking shelter amid the strong winds and floodwaters.Elsewhere in the province, Wenzhou authorities have relocated some 900,000 residents and opened more than 1,000 emergency shelters, while about 390,000 people have been evacuated from their homes in the city of Taizhou.In the coastal province of Fujian, maritime authorities have suspended dozens of passenger ferry routes and halted more than 100 offshore construction projects.The storm moved over a long distance of 6,000km before making landfall, suggesting a lifespan of more than three times that of an average typhoon, according to China's state broadcaster CCTV. It also has a massive circulation size and intense rainfall capacity, CCTV reported.

schema.headline: Typhoon Dolphin: China evacuates more than 1 million people as massive storm arrives

title: Ecuador charges ex-minister over presidential candidate assassination case
description: Prosecutors in Ecuador have charged a former interior minister and six others on suspicion of being involved in the assassination of a presidential ca
body: Prosecutors in Ecuador have charged a former interior minister and six others on suspicion of being involved in the assassination of a presidential candidate in 2023.José Serrano and the head of cartel Los Lobos, Wilmer "Pipo" Chavarria, were implicated in the murder of Fernando Villavicencio at a campaign event in the capital, Quito, days before the election.Five people linked to the criminal gang were jailed over the hit in 2024, while Pipo was captured in Spain last year, having faked his own death.Villavicencio, a journalist turned prominent legislator, was known for his anti-corruption stance and was one of few candidates to allege links between organised crime and government officials.He had continued to appear at public campaigns after being given a security detail due to his receiving a number of death threats.Daniel Noboa, who ultimately went on to win the election and become Ecuador's president, has taken a hardline military approach to combatting crime gangs. The five convicted over Villavicencio's murder in 2024 were said to have orchestrated the hit. The alleged gunman was shot dead at the scene, while six other men were found murdered in prison while awaiting trial.The seven named by the Ecuadorean Attorney General's Office on Saturday were accused of playing an indirect role in the killing - many of whom had links to Los Lobos, or "The Wolves", one of the nation's most powerful criminal gangs.Five of these were now considered fugitives, it said.Serrano and Xavier Jordán were currently located in the US, former assemblyman Ronny Aleaga was in Venezuela, while Pipo remained in Spain with an extradition request pending. The Attorney General's Office has requested Interpol red notices for their capture and extradition.Ángel Esteban Aguilar, also known as Lobo Menor, was arrested in Mexico City in March and returned to Ecuador after a red notice was issued over the murder of Villavicencio.

schema.headline: Ecuador charges ex-minister over presidential candidate assassination case

title: World's oceans hit record-high July temperatures
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByJessica RawnsleyThe world's oceans hit their hottest ever recorded temperatures for July, partly fuelled by developing El
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByJessica RawnsleyThe world's oceans hit their hottest ever recorded temperatures for July, partly fuelled by developing El Niño conditions in the Pacific, according to the EU's climate monitoring service.The average sea surface temperature (SST) outside the world's polar regions - between 60 degrees north and 60 degrees south - was 20.96C last month, beating the previous high of 20.89C, set in 2023.Last month was the joint second-warmest July globally on record, with temperatures 1.47C above the estimated pre-industrial average, according to the Copernicus Climate Change Service.Meanwhile, Western Europe experienced its hottest ever June and July, with prolonged hot and dry conditions fuelling extreme wildfires across the region.Elsewhere, the UK is braced for its fifth heatwave of the year this week, as persistent dry weather puts further pressure on water supplies and could see more areas officially declared in drought.Around Europe, sea surface temperatures in July reached record highs along the Atlantic coast and in the western Mediterranean, contributing to widespread strong and severe marine heatwaves.Sea temperatures remained exceptionally high across much of the tropical Pacific, where El Niño conditions are developing and forecast to strengthen in the coming months. El Niño is a natural weather pattern in the Pacific that combined with human-driven global warming can cause temperature spikes and more extreme weather.Oceans are a vital regulator of the climate, absorbing most of the excess heat generated by greenhouse gas emissions and producing half of Earth's oxygen.The greatest effect of ocean warming is on sea level rise. As seawater warms it expands, and this thermal expansion accounts for roughly a third of sea level rise recorded by scientists to date. That water encroaches on low-lying coasts and island nations.Hotter seas are also driving longer and fiercer marine heatwaves, which have bleached coral reefs on a mass scale and decimated kelp forests and fisheries.Warmer ocean surfaces also evaporate more heat and moisture into the air, intensifying tropical storms and loading them with heavier rainfall.'Climate change is intensifying heat extremes'Western Europe is experiencing an exceptional run of extreme heat - with record-breaking temperatures in June and July, and some areas facing their third or fourth heat wave since May.The average temperature across western Europe for June and July was 21.62C - 2.79C above average and the highest for the two-month period."July 2026 was the third consecutive month of exceptional heat in western Europe," said Samantha Burgess, strategic lead for climate at the European Center for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts.Persistent high-pressure systems trapped heat over the region, she said, while dry soils reduced the ability to provide natural cooling."This is a clear example of how climate change is intensifying heat extremes, with heat and drought increasingly reinforcing one another," she added.France, Spain, parts of Germany and the UK recorded exceptionally low rainfall and/or soil moisture, while soil moisture levels across much of western Europe were significantly lower than in 2022, when the region experienced severe drought.River levels have been much lower than average - in some places exceptionally low -with the Seine, Rhine and Danube among those particularly affected.Low flows exacerbate pressure on water supplies and irrigation, aquatic ecosystems, river transport and energy production.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Some rivers in Europe have recorded extremely low water levels, including the Danube The prolonged hot and dry conditions have created favourable conditions for wildfires, with massive wildfires raging across western Europe last month and "exceptional activity" in terms of the area burned and smoke and emissions generated."Climate change is increasingly bringing the kinds of hot and dry conditions that favour large, high-intensity wildfires in southern Europe while extended the fire season northwards," said Laurence Rouil, director of the Copernicus Atmosphere Monitoring Service.Larger fires produce more smoke and inject it higher into the atmosphere, allowing it to travel much further, he said.That means countries that experience relatively few wildfires could be increasingly affected by smoke traveling long distances.Extreme weather 'new normal'Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, European wildfires haven been called "completely unprecedented" this summerIn the UK, meanwhile, the prolonged dry spell is increasing pressure on already-stretched water supplies.England and Wales recorded their driest July since records began 190 years ago, according to the Met Office, while large parts of England and all of Wales have already been officially declared in drought.The Environment Agency has warned that more areas of England could be declared in drought if dry conditions persist.Weather that was once considered extreme is becoming the "new normal", according to the latest Met Office report on the UK's climate.Its latest assessment found that the hottest day of the year in southern England is now 4.5C warmer than it was between 1961 and 1990."We are right now living in a time of historic and unprecedented change," said Mike Kendon, Met Office climate information scientist, adding that "evidence shows the climate of the 20th century has now gone".Scientists say El Niño may temporarily push global temperatures even higher. Its effects are being felt against a backdrop of man-made warming, particularly the burning of fossil fuels.The world is now about 1.4C warmer on average than it was in the late 19th Century.

schema.headline: World's oceans hit record-high July temperatures
